newsitem.title: SUDAN: Sudan air ban will halt aid to millions - U.N.
newsitem.headline: Sudan air ban will halt aid to millions - U.N.

text.p: United Nations sanctions on Sudan could paralyse aid for millions of people in Africa's largest country who are dependent on food and medicine distributed by aircraft, a U.N. official said.

Claude Bruderlein, a U.N. humanitarian affairs policy adviser, said the U.N. next month will discuss how and when to enforce resolution 1070, which prohibits all aircraft registered in Sudan, including the country's flag carrier and government-owned or operated planes from flying out of Sudan.

"This is the first time that the Security Council has studied the humanitarian impact before imposing the sanctions because of the bad experience in Iraq," Bruderlein told Reuters on Wednesday. The U.N. in 1990 imposed sanctions on Baghdad for invading Kuwait.

"What I will tell the (U.N.) undersecretary is if the sanctions are imposed...the Security Council would have to take responsibility for the suspension of the relief operation. It's a very serious decision," he added.
Because of the hardship caused by the sanctions on Iraq the United Nations is allowing it to export $2 billion worth of oil every six months to buy food, medicine and other humanitarian supplies.
The Sudan ban was passed in August as punishment for what the U.N. said was its airline's role in flying to Ethiopia gunmen who tried to kill Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak in 1995.
The U.N. has already imposed a limited travel and diplomatic ban on Sudan for not extraditing the three Islamist gunmen but Khartoum says it does not know where they are.
Bruderlein said that independent aircraft registered in Sudan would be hit because they would not be able to fly abroad for maintenance. Sudan only has facilities for routine checks.
This means aid agencies which rely on such aircraft would be unable to distribute aid to remote areas hit by civil war and drought in the country, one of the poorest in the world.

Sudan been fighting rebels in the south since 1983 and it now accuses Eritrea and Ethiopia of supporting these rebels, who are currently waging an offensive in the east. Both states deny any part in the fighting.
A poor road network, rainy season floods and the rebel war make many areas in Sudan inaccessible by land.
"... if sanctions ground the aircraft it will paralyse relief operations in the war-affected regions in the south, and the consquences could be dramatic," Bruderlein said.
Asked how many people were dependent on relief for survival, Bruderlein said: "In terms of millions".

Philip Clarke, World Food Programme country director, said the WFP pre-positions food to the south by plane and then ferries it to remote areas by barge along the Nile. They usually start in mid-March when the ban is likely to start.
"Distribution has to be by air to those places, otherwise there is no distribution of such things as medicine and food," Clarke said.
At least five independent air carriers registered in Sudan ferry mostly cargo throughout the country, Bruderlein said.
The sanctions would also make it difficult for Sudanese needing medical treatement not available in Sudan to go abroad, which they can now do at subsidised prices on Sudan Airways, Bruderlein said.
Unlike Libya and Iraq, on which the U.N. has imposed sanctions, foreign trade plays a relatively small role in Sudan's agriculture-dominated economy.
